title: The whole world in his mouth

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when did something last make you stop and say wow?
options: lovely. this story is one long wow.
then this one’s for you. look closely.
then you’ll understand the mother in this story.

steps.line: In Hindu tradition, Krishna is God come to earth. As a toddler in a village of cowherds, he was a handful. One day the boys saw him eating dirt.
His big brother Balarama and the other boys ran to his mother, Yashoda: “Krishna ate mud!”
Yashoda took his little hand. Krishna looked up, all innocence. “I didn’t! They’re fibbing. Look in my mouth if you don’t believe me.”

steps.q: Krishna opens his mouth wide. Inside: stars, oceans, the whole universe. What else does Yashoda spot in there?
o: The great war still to come
Every god, bowing to her son
steps.why: Her village, and Yashoda herself, looking in. The Bhagavata says she saw the whole universe, and her own self inside it.

steps.line: She looked, and saw everything: sky and stars, mountains and oceans, fire, wind, the moon. And inside it all, her own village, and herself.

steps.q: Why does the story put Yashoda’s own village, and Yashoda herself, inside his mouth?
o: Even the one looking is held inside it
To show that she was only dreaming
To prove the boys were telling the truth
steps.why: She isn’t outside the wonder looking in. She’s part of it. So is everyone.

steps.line: She was shaken. Was this a dream? Who was this child? Then, the old text says, he let her forget, and wrapped her in a mother’s love again.
She lifted him onto her lap and held him close. Just her little boy again, in the middle of everything.

steps.q: Yashoda wasn’t Krishna’s birth mother. Why was he raised in a cowherd village?
o: His birth parents had died young
To hide him from a murderous king
steps.why: He was born in a Mathura prison to Devaki and Vasudeva, and carried across the river by night to hide from King Kamsa. Yashoda raised him as her own.

steps.line: Today: a night sky far from the city, so full of stars it looks fake. For a moment you get small, in the good way.
steps.label: today

steps.q: The toddler had another famous nickname in the village. What?
steps.why: Makhan chor, the butter thief. Stories of him raiding the neighbors’ butter pots are some of the most loved in Hinduism.

say: here’s what i love. yashoda looks into a toddler’s mouth and finds everything. then she’s a mom again, holding him close. both are true.
in hindu teaching, the divine is vast enough to hold every star, and near enough to sit on your lap. awe and love belong together. look up, feel small, and come back down a little warmer.

steps.q: Why might the story have Krishna let Yashoda forget what she saw?
o: So she wouldn’t tell the village
Such awe would crowd out a mother’s love
So she’d stop worrying about the mud
steps.why: She could only hold him close as a mother if she wasn’t overwhelmed. Awe, then love.

today.say: hindus speak of darshan: seeing the divine, and being seen. today, take a minute of it with the biggest thing you can see: the sky, a tree, the clouds. let it be big. then, like yashoda, come back and hold someone close, simply.
options: good. it’s there every night, free.
then close your eyes and remember the biggest sky you’ve stood under.

tomorrow.title: Back before sunset.
tomorrow.line: a tyrant sentences a man to death. his best friend takes his place, and waits.

card.keepWhy: The vast and the near, both at once.
sources: Bhagavata Purana 10.8.32–45: Rama (Balarama) and the other cowherd boys tell Yashoda that Krishna has eaten earth; she takes him by the hand and scolds him; he denies it and tells her to look in his mouth; she sees the whole universe, the sky, the directions, mountains, islands and oceans, the earth, wind, fire, moon and stars, and Vraja and herself; she wonders whether it is a dream or a divine illusion; the Lord spreads his maya in the form of a mother’s love, she forgets, and takes him on her lap.

check: “In Hindu tradition, Krishna is God come to earth”: many traditions call him an avatar of Vishnu, others the Supreme himself. Confirm the wording.
Today: darshan is usually the sight of a deity, a holy person or place; using it for a sky full of stars widens it, as many teachers do for nature. Confirm the wording.
